doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Harlem in the Himalayas at the Rubin Museum; museum growth
summary: The Rubin Museum concert series, a Kenny Davern story, and hiring staff with Batiste and McBride.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: of that came all of the other programs: Jazz for Curious Listeners, and Jazz for Curious Readers, and I can’t even remember them all. And then we started producing a concert series at the Rubin Museum of Art called Harlem in the Himalayas. Because the Rubin Museum of Art is dedicated to the culture of the Himalayas.

Yeah, yeah. Well the way it happened was there was a man named Donald Rubin who made a lot of money in health insurance. And he had more money than he knew what to do with. And he was nuts about, he was dedicated to Himalayan and culture and spirituality. So he built this vanity museum down on 18th Street I believe it is, off of Seventh Avenue, and he hired all the right people and got a brilliant programmer or a brilliant designer, and his vanity project wound up becoming one of the hippest, smartest, most popular museums in Manhattan. I mean who’d of thought that it might happen. So I went down to meet him because Len had met him at the urologist’s office, and started to pitch a program to him and he said, “What should we call it?” I said, “Harlem in the Himalayas.” And he said, “What does that mean?” I said, “I have no idea.” And this program went on for several years, it won some awards for best programming, and I’m proud of it. If you look at it, we must have done 150 concerts or something like that. And the idea was that whoever came down, whether it was Dizzy Reese or whether it was Jack Walrath or whether it was, I mean, I can’t even start to name the names, all kinds of young contemporary musicians and famous people from other countries, the idea was that one of the tunes that you played would relate to the Himalayan exhibits in the museum. Either you’d write a tune, I mean I remember one guy came in and played “Caravan” but that was a one-off. That never happened again. Or as Kenny Davern used to say, “CarAvan.” Did you interview him?

Oh boy do I miss him, I wish he was around. But anyway, yeah, Kenny told me, he said one time he was on one of those jazz cruises and they told the band, you know, you’ll eat with the customers, everything. Well of course every time they went to eat in the restaurant they never got called. Their table never got called. And so there they are with all these great guys and they’re just ignoring him so he told me he says, “Man I went up to the microphone to announce and I said, ‘Christ, party of 12.’” Anyway so the Rubin Museum of Art, so the museum slowly grew, I mean for a long time it was just me and one other person, and then two other people, and then eventually it got to the point where we had three people. And then eventually we got to the point where I realized that I was not the right person anymore. I mean I was writing the checks and opening the door and putting up the chairs, and at some point, like we really needed, especially if we wanted to go to the next level of development and raising money, it wasn’t enough to say oh isn’t © Fillius Jazz Archive -32-

this wonderful. There’s two people, boy, they do everything you know. Who wants to give real money to that? So the board and I decided you know it was time to really hire an administrator, administrative staff, and now we have a full time staff of four or five, a great administrator, a lot of consultants, and our artistic directors are John Bastiste and Christian McBride. And we’re about to enter our third decade.
